name: Rosa Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and this interview is confidential. What does a usual day at work involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am a junior conveyor operator at Pine Gate mine, checking the belt and clearing small blockages with the crew. I started after years caring for my mother, so I am still learning the equipment at fifty-eight. I finished secondary school and use an AI app every day to turn my rough shift notes into a checklist. My partner and I have grown children, but less than one month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the app saves me ten minutes on notes, and that is fine if the belt work stays ours. I would still walk the conveyor before every start. A tidy checklist does not remove a jam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The picture sounds gentle, but my pay is low and we have almost nothing put aside. The mine sometimes cuts a shift after a breakdown, and there are few other mines nearby. I would still worry about next month’s bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my scheduled belt shifts and check the app’s lists against the machine each morning. I would put any overtime into a separate bill account this month. In the first year I would keep asking for shifts rather than assuming a small AI change made us safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious already. The word plateau would not pay our electricity bill if a shift disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill is tightest now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill rises when our heating runs all night. My partner and I can cover this month, but one lost shift would eat the small balance. I would ask for overtime before borrowing from our daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the app get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once put a belt noise under cleaning instead of inspection. I changed the note and showed the supervisor. The AI checklist is a prompt, not my eyes.

say: I would use the **AI checklist** for notes while still walking the conveyor before each start.
I would ask for **steady shifts** because small time savings do not pay our bills.
think: My **low pay** and tiny savings make one missed shift a problem even if AI changes little.
Few **nearby mines** mean I cannot easily replace the job.
do: **Keep** taking scheduled Pine Gate conveyor shifts and checking the belt.
**Compare** AI checklists against the machine each morning.
**Put** any overtime into the household bill account.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills and missed shifts.
S0.quote: The AI checklist is a prompt, not my eyes.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** makes the mild picture stressful before any larger AI threat.
She uses **AI daily** but checks its output against physical belt sounds.
She would put **overtime** toward bills, not claim it builds a secure savings fund.

steps.text: Keep taking scheduled Pine Gate conveyor shifts
Check AI belt lists against the conveyor each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software might change the mine office first, and the belt still needs people for now. I would ask our union steward to watch shifts and training places. New targets should not mean skipping a conveyor walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch and purchasing could be cut before my own job, but the mine may push us to do more with fewer people. I am a junior worker, and I cannot pretend my place is secure if shifts shrink. My partner’s pay is irregular too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI shift board with the dispatcher during the first month. I would keep a notebook of belt checks and hours, then take any lost shifts to the union steward. I would call the nearby repair shop about weekend cleaning work only if the hours actually fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a screen quickly, but I cannot learn my way out of an unpaid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the steward to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the roster numbers before and after the software starts. If junior shifts were lost, the union could press for paid training or fair sharing of hours. I would bring my notebook, not just a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour runs it and sometimes needs someone to clean parts. I have not asked for work yet. It would be a few hours, not a replacement for mine pay.

I would protect the **conveyor walk** against tighter targets.
think: As a **junior worker**, I could lose hours even while conveyor work remains hands-on.
My partner’s **irregular pay** leaves little room for a missed week.

**Call** the nearby repair shop about weekend cleaning if conveyor hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about hours shrinking despite her ability to learn new software.
S1.quote: I can learn a screen quickly, but I cannot learn my way out of an unpaid week.
fieldNote: She sees **office planning** changing before conveyor work, yet expects pressure on junior hours.
Her willingness to learn AI is real, but **income risk** remains high with irregular household pay.
The repair shop is only a **fallback enquiry** if shifts actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes planning, not the conveyor motor in that year. Capable robots arrive around 2031, and we need a union agreement before the mine tries them. I would ask for paid training for junior operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when robots become capable. If the mine bought robot conveyor crews then, I might lose pay before I could afford to retire. We have less than a month saved, and my partner’s work would not cover both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union steward for an emergency income plan and paid training places this month. I would enrol in a paid equipment inspection course if the mine offered a real post at the end. After 2028 I would keep checking the belt while the mine still used people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lie awake thinking about being sixty-three with an empty bank account and no pension large enough to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the weekend bus trips to see friends and keep the fare for food. I would not stop visiting my mother’s grave altogether; we could go less often. It is a small saving, but there is no large spare expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you call if wages stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter would take our call, but she has rent of her own. I would ask the union first about any income bridge. I would not make our daughter the household plan.

I would press the **union** for paid training and an income bridge.
think: At **sixty-three** when robots become capable, I might lose pay before affordable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robots gives us time to bargain. The union should get paid training started before junior shifts disappear. I would volunteer to test any new inspection checklist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive in 2034. The longer gap could let me build an inspection skill, but low pay means I still cannot assume a comfortable retirement. If the mine cuts my shifts early, the extra years vanish for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid inspection course next year if a real mine opening was posted. I would test the AI inspection checklist against belt faults this winter and share errors with the supervisor. I would also put a little from each full week’s pay into a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have more time to try something, but my bank balance still decides how much risk I can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the pay from one extra hour each full week, if overtime stays available. I would check our bills with my partner before promising a number. A week with fewer shifts would leave nothing to transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you report first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool sometimes calls a hot bearing a cleaning job. I would photograph the temperature reading and ask maintenance to confirm it. I do not want a faster form to hide a fire risk.

I would test an **AI checklist** against real belt faults and report misses.
think: At about **sixty-six** when capable robots arrive, retirement may still be unaffordable.
The extra time helps only while **full shifts** keep paying our bills.

**Transfer** one extra hour’s pay from full weeks to an emergency account if bills allow.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to learn but little money for risk.
S3.quote: A week with fewer shifts would leave nothing to transfer.
fieldNote: She would be **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years to thinking AI and about thirteen to capable robots gives the mine time to plan fairly. I would ask the union to keep junior workers in that plan. A long runway is useful only if people can keep earning during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight at thinking AI in 2036 and around seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I hope to retire before then, but less than a month of savings means I cannot promise it. Our pension figures matter more than a promised robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my conveyor shifts and ask for a pension statement this year. I would sit down with my partner to compare it with our bills, then ask a local advice worker about options if it fell short. I would keep using the AI checklist for faults while working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The robot date is far away, but the question of paying for retirement is already in our kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension statement is lower than you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask about working fewer shifts later rather than stopping at once. The mine would have to agree to that schedule. I would not call retirement secure before seeing the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still seek new training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the mine offered paid time and a job I could actually do. At sixty-eight I would not borrow for a certificate. I would rather learn the inspection tasks I already touch.

say: I would ask the **union** to keep junior workers in the mine’s long-term plan.
I would say a **long runway** matters only if wages continue during it.
think: At about **seventy-one** when capable robots arrive, I hope to be retired but cannot assume it.
My **pension statement** will tell us more about security than the scenario date.
do: **Keep** conveyor shifts and request a pension statement this year.
**Compare** pension income with household bills and seek advice if it falls short.
**Use** AI fault checklists while still working.
feel: **Anxious** because retirement funding remains uncertain even with a distant robot date.
S4.quote: Our pension figures matter more than a promised robot date.
fieldNote: The robot date at about **seventy-one** may follow retirement, but retirement itself is uncertain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable conveyor robots could arrive around 2031 before I can afford retirement. A paid inspection place tied to a real job and an income bridge would help. The union should get those terms in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to a worker who came into mining late after caring for family. I do not have twenty years of mine pension behind me. I can learn new tools, but I cannot invent missing savings.

headlineQuote: I can learn new tools, but I cannot invent missing savings.
portrait: Rosa Nakamura is a **58-year-old** junior conveyor operator at Pine Gate mine who entered after years caring for her mother.
She uses **AI daily** for shift notes, but checks every suggested fault against the physical belt.
Her **low pay** and less than a month saved make even AI Plateau stressful when a shift is lost.
Fast robots could reach her before affordable **retirement**; more warning helps only if paid work and training continue.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable conveyor robots could arrive around 2031 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid inspection place** tied to a real job and an income bridge written into a union agreement would help.
